# Rockwell Automation pairs AI with decades of shop floor know-how so workers can solve glitches faster

##### By 

- Lim Ai Leen

September 24, 2026

 

For engineering assistant Mangleswaran Mahalingam, getting a stalled machine up and running used to mean leafing through hundreds of pages in a manual to find an error code and its recommended fix. If that didn’t work, he’d have to track down a colleague who’d resolved a similar snag before. It was a painstaking process, often involving trial and error.

Today, however, he can access that collective knowledge in seconds.

Since October 2025, technicians overseeing hundreds of machines at Rockwell Automation’s Singapore site have been using the GenAI-Powered Maintenance Copilot, an in-house AI assistant trained on its workers’ expert knowledge, data from its manufacturing software and the machines’ instruction manuals.

results.title: From AI Proof of Concept to Production: A Tiered Rollout at a $340M Agricultural Equipment Distributor

From AI Proof of Concept to Production: A Tiered Rollout at a $340M Agricultural Equipment Distributor

# From AI Proof of Concept to Production: A Tiered Rollout at a $340M Agricultural Equipment Distributor

Ed Hitchcock

Sep 8

By Ed Hitchcock, Enterprise AI Systems Architect, SupplyTech Solutions

Most mid-market distributors we meet have already run one or two AI experiments. A ChatGPT pilot in customer service. A Copilot rollout that nobody used after week three. A vendor demo that promised "predictive parts ordering" and never made it past the sandbox. When these fail, the reflex is to blame the technology or the company. Both are usually wrong. What failed was scoping. The team ran an AI proof of concept without a defined path to what comes after it.

This post walks through a 26-week engagement with an agricultural equipment distributor that avoided that trap by treating the AI proof of concept as the first tier of a three-tier path, not a standalone experiment. We call the tiers Lite, Advanced, and Expert. Each tier is useful on its own. Each assumes the previous one has stabilized. Each is defined by the enterprise mechanics it adds, not the model version underneath it.

# Sultan’s AI Agents Pay Off for FavTrip

 Sep 8 2026 

After one of his artificial intelligence (AI) agents catches a major error, Sultan shares his playbook and future goals.

One of Babir Sultan’s artificial intelligence (AI) agents recently caught a $25,000 error.

Earlier this year, Sultan, founder and CEO of FavTrip, a three-store convenience chain in Missouri, identified four pain points he needed to solve for his business. He assigned an AI agent to each issue. One tracks snacking trends and makes suggestions for which snacks to stock. The second drafts posts for FavTrip’s three social media channels. The third is a billing agent that reconciles weekly gas invoices, and the fourth AI agent messages job applicants for open interviews.

Sultan said it all comes down to efficiency. The AI agents free employees from time-consuming tasks, allowing them to focus their energy on other responsibilities in the store.

# Uniper feeds Celonis context into Microsoft Copilot to energize HR AI agents 

 By Derek du Preez September 9, 2026

Summary: 
: German energy giant Uniper is taking a pragmatic approach to the adoption of agentic AI - assessing the partners it has already, thinking about context enablement with Celonis, and bringing the tooling to where employees are - in Microsoft Teams. 

 

Given the complexities in achieving agentic AI success this early on in the technology adoption cycle, it’s perhaps surprising that a company like Uniper - a highly regulated organization in the EU - is seeing results in a function like HR, the data for which can be categorized as a ‘high risk’ by EU regulations. However, what’s perhaps less surprising is that the success is being achieved through a very pragmatic approach to adoption: collaboration between different teams, delivering the technology where employees are already working, starting small with use cases, and recognizing the potential of existing vendor partnerships, rather than chasing shiny new things.
